claim: Episodic memory, particularly the ability to form and retrieve associations between multiple event elements, declines with age.
source: Episodic memory – in particular the ability to form and retrieve associations between multiple event elements that comprise past experiences – declines with age (Spencer and Raz, 1995; Rönnlund et al., 2005; Old and Naveh-Benjamin, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on age-related memory decline.

claim: Retrieval of an episodic memory relies critically on hippocampal-dependent pattern completion.
source: Retrieval of an episodic memory relies critically on hippocampal-dependent pattern completion, which entails reactivation of a stored memory trace by the hippocampus in response to a partial cue, leading to replay of cortical activity patterns that were present at the time of memory encoding (Marr, 1971; McClelland et al., 1995; Tanaka et al., 2014; Staresina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical models and empirical evidence cited in the introduction.

claim: Pattern completion entails reactivation of a stored memory trace by the hippocampus in response to a partial cue, leading to replay of cortical activity patterns that were present at the time of memory encoding.
source: Retrieval of an episodic memory relies critically on hippocampal-dependent pattern completion, which entails reactivation of a stored memory trace by the hippocampus in response to a partial cue, leading to replay of cortical activity patterns that were present at the time of memory encoding (Marr, 1971; McClelland et al., 1995; Tanaka et al., 2014; Staresina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the theoretical mechanism of pattern completion and is supported by citations to computational and empirical work.

claim: In vivo measures of pattern completion are linked to episodic remembering.
source: Given observed links between in vivo measures of pattern completion and episodic remembering (Nakazawa et al., 2002; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 2014), and evidence of altered hippocampal function with age (Lister and Barnes, 2009; Leal and Yassa, 2013), changes in hippocampal pattern completion may play an important role in explaining age-related impairments in episodic memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior empirical studies linking pattern completion measures to memory.

claim: Hippocampal function is altered with age.
source: Given observed links between in vivo measures of pattern completion and episodic remembering (Nakazawa et al., 2002; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 2014), and evidence of altered hippocampal function with age (Lister and Barnes, 2009; Leal and Yassa, 2013), changes in hippocampal pattern completion may play an important role in explaining age-related impairments in episodic memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on age-related changes in hippocampal function.

claim: Changes in hippocampal pattern completion may play an important role in explaining age-related impairments in episodic memory.

evidence: This is a hypothesis statement based on prior evidence, indicating speculation about the role of pattern completion in age-related memory decline.

claim: Hippocampal pattern completion is associated with an increase in hippocampal univariate activity.
source: Functional MRI (fMRI) studies in younger adults suggest that hippocampal pattern completion is associated with at least two key neural markers: (a) an increase in hippocampal univariate activity (Eldridge et al., 2000; Dobbins et al., 2003; Yonelinas et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies in younger adults.

claim: Hippocampal pattern completion is associated with cortical reinstatement of content-specific activity patterns present during encoding.
source: Functional MRI (fMRI) studies in younger adults suggest that hippocampal pattern completion is associated with at least two key neural markers: (a) an increase in hippocampal univariate activity (Eldridge et al., 2000; Dobbins et al., 2003; Yonelinas et al., 2005) and (b) cortical reinstatement of content-specific activity patterns present during encoding (Nyberg et al., 2000; Wheeler et al., 2000; Kahn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies in younger adults.

claim: Multivariate pattern analyses reveal evidence for cortical reinstatement of categorical event features during successful recollection.
source: Multivariate pattern analyses — machine learning classification (Norman et al., 2006) and pattern similarity (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) — reveal evidence for cortical reinstatement of categorical event features (Polyn et al., 2005; Johnson and Rugg, 2007; Gordon et al., 2014) and event-specific details (Staresina et al., 2012; Ritchey et al., 2013; Kuhl and Chun, 2014) during successful recollection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies using multivariate pattern analysis methods.

claim: Multivariate pattern analyses reveal evidence for cortical reinstatement of event-specific details during successful recollection.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies using multivariate pattern analysis methods.

claim: Trial-wise fluctuations in hippocampal univariate retrieval activity are related to the strength of cortical reinstatement.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing covariation between hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement.

claim: Both hippocampal activity and reinstatement strength are related to associative retrieval performance.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing relationships between neural measures and memory performance.

claim: Controlling for age and sex, VTC category-level reinstatement strength was a significant predictor of delayed recall score (β = 0.21, p <0.01).
source: Controlling for age and sex, hippocampal activity (β = 0.19, p < 0.01; Figure 5g) and VTC category-level reinstatement strength (β = 0.21, p <0.01; Figure 5h) were significant predictors of delayed recall score
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis showing the relationship between VTC reinstatement and standardized memory test performance, visualized in Figure 5h.

claim: The relationship between ANG category-level reinstatement strength and delayed recall score did not reach significance (β = 0.14, p = 0.11).
source: the relationship with ANG category-level reinstatement strength did not reach significance (β = 0.14, p = 0.11; Figure 5i
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis showing no significant relationship between ANG reinstatement and standardized memory test performance, visualized in Figure 5i.

claim: Hippocampal activity and VTC category-level reinstatement strength explained unique variance in delayed recall performance (hippocampus: β = 0.16, p < 0.05; VTC: β = 0.20, p < 0.05, adjusted R2 = 0.231).
source: Further, as for exemplar-specific recall, we found that hippocampal activity and VTC category-level reinstatement strength explained unique variance in delayed recall performance (hippocampus: β = 0.16, p < 0.05; VTC: β = 0.20, p < 0.05, adjusted R2 = 0.231).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical regression showing independent contributions of hippocampal activity and VTC reinstatement to standardized memory test performance.

claim: When delayed recall score was added to the full model, this measure explained additional variance in exemplar-specific recall (model comparison: F(1,94) = 7.45, p < 0.01, adjusted R2 = 0.485).
source: When delayed recall score was added to the full model (see Table 2, Step 5), this measure explained additional variance in exemplar-specific recall (model comparison: F(1,94) = 7.45, p < 0.01, adjusted R2 = 0.485)
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical regression showing that standardized memory test performance explains additional variance.

claim: Hippocampal activity and VTC category-level reinstatement strength remained significant predictors of exemplar-specific recall even after adding delayed recall score to the model (hippocampus: β = 0.335, p < 10−5; VTC reinstatement: β = 0.377, p < 10−5).
source: but hippocampal activity and VTC category-level reinstatement strength remained significant predictors (hippocampus: β = 0.335, p < 10−5; VTC reinstatement: β = 0.377, p < 10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical regression showing that neural measures explain variance beyond standardized memory tests.

claim: Individual differences in the integrity of pattern completion processes, indexed by univariate and pattern-based task-related fMRI metrics, explain variance in memory performance across established hippocampal-dependent assays of episodic memory.
source: Together, these results support the hypothesis that individual differences in the integrity of pattern completion processes, indexed by univariate and pattern-based task-related fMRI metrics, explain variance in memory performance across established hippocampal-dependent assays of episodic memory, and do so in a manner that is not captured by simple standardized neuropsychological tests.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings that neural measures predict both task-based and standardized memory performance.

claim: fMRI indices of pattern completion explain variance in memory performance in a manner that is not captured by simple standardized neuropsychological tests.
source: Together, these results support the hypothesis that individual differences in the integrity of pattern completion processes, indexed by univariate and pattern-based task-related fMRI metrics, explain variance in memory performance across established hippocampal-dependent assays of episodic memory, and do so in a manner that is not captured by simple standardized neuropsychological tests.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that neural measures remain significant predictors even after controlling for standardized test performance.

claim: The present analyses of trial-level brain-behaviour relationships significantly build on work in younger adults, demonstrating that trial-wise relationships between hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement and between each of these neural measures and memory behaviour are present later in the lifespan.
source: The present analyses of trial-level brain-behaviour relationships significantly build on work in younger adults (Gordon et al., 2014; Gagnon et al., 2019), demonstrating that trial-wise relationships (a) between hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement and (b) between each of these neural measures and memory behaviour are present later in the lifespan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trial-wise findings in older adults, which extend prior work in younger adults.

claim: The results are consistent with models of episodic retrieval wherein hippocampal pattern completion, triggered by partial cues, drives reinstatement of event representations in the cortex, which supports episodic remembering and memory-guided decision making.
source: While directionality is difficult to establish with fMRI, these results are consistent with models of episodic retrieval wherein hippocampal pattern completion, triggered by partial cues, drives reinstatement of event representations in the cortex, which supports episodic remembering and memory-guided decision making (Marr, 1971; McClelland et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationships between hippocampal activity, cortical reinstatement, and memory behavior, interpreted in the context of theoretical models.

claim: Category-level cortical reinstatement partially mediates the relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success.
source: Further bolstering this interpretation, we demonstrate that (a) category-level cortical reinstatement partially mediates the relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis presented in the results.

claim: The relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success was qualitatively strongest in DG/CA3, consistent with a key role of CA3 in initiating pattern-completion dependent retrieval.
source: and (b) the relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success was qualitatively strongest in DG/CA3, consistent with a key role of CA3 in initiating pattern-completion dependent retrieval (Marr, 1971; McClelland et al., 1995; Nakazawa et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2014; Staresina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by subfield analysis showing the strongest effect in DG/CA3, interpreted in the context of theoretical models.

claim: The trial-wise relationship between hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement did not vary as a function of age.
source: Moreover, the present results provide novel evidence for stability in the trial-wise relationship between hippocampal activity and (a) cortical reinstatement and (b) associative retrieval success, as neither relationship varied as a function of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by mixed effects modeling showing no significant age moderation of the trial-wise relationship.

claim: The trial-wise relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success did not vary as a function of age.
source: Moreover, the present results provide novel evidence for stability in the trial-wise relationship between hippocampal activity and (a) cortical reinstatement and (b) associative retrieval success, as neither relationship varied as a function of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by mixed effects modeling showing no significant age moderation of the trial-wise relationship.

claim: The positive relationship between the magnitude of hippocampal activity during associative hits and associative memory performance complements and builds on prior work.
source: Consistent with the observed trial-level relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success, we also demonstrate a positive relationship between the magnitude of hippocampal activity during associative hits and associative memory performance. Our findings complement and build on prior work (de Chastelaine et al., 2016)
evidence: This is an inference based on the individual differences findings, interpreted in the context of prior research.

claim: The positive relationship between hippocampal activity and memory performance was observed across hippocampal subfields, including DG/CA3.
source: as we demonstrate that this effect was observed across hippocampal subfields, including DG/CA3, and did not vary significantly as a function of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by subfield analysis showing the relationship across multiple subfields.

claim: The positive relationship between hippocampal activity and memory performance did not vary significantly as a function of age.
source: as we demonstrate that this effect was observed across hippocampal subfields, including DG/CA3, and did not vary significantly as a function of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by regression analysis showing no significant age moderation.

claim: The results are compatible with proposals that the relationship between hippocampal 'recollection success' effects and memory performance remains stable across the lifespan.
source: These results are compatible with proposals that the relationship between hippocampal 'recollection success' effects and memory performance remains stable across the lifespan (de Chastelaine et al., 2016)
evidence: This is an inference based on the age-invariant relationship between hippocampal activity and memory, interpreted in the context of prior proposals.

claim: The results are compatible with proposals that preservation of hippocampal function is important for the maintenance of episodic memory in older adults over time.
source: as well as more broadly with proposals that preservation of hippocampal function is important for the maintenance of episodic memory in older adults over time (Persson et al., 2012; Pudas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive relationship between hippocampal activity and memory performance, interpreted in the context of prior proposals.

claim: A negative relationship between hippocampal retrieval activity and memory performance has been observed in older adults in some studies.
source: We note, however, that a negative relationship between hippocampal retrieval activity and memory performance has also been observed in older adults (e.g., Carr et al., 2017; Reagh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies showing different patterns of results.

claim: Differences across studies may be related to the paradigms and/or contrasts employed, image resolution, or the make-up of the study population.
source: Differences across studies may be related to (a) the paradigms and/or contrasts employed (e.g., associative recollection vs. lure discrimination), (b) image resolution (e.g., individual subfields vs. the whole hippocampus), or (c) the make-up of the study population (e.g., cognitively normal or cognitively impaired; Dickerson and Sperling, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation about potential reasons for differences across studies.

claim: Trial-wise indices of reinstatement strength were tightly linked to memory behaviour, including response accuracy and speed.
source: The present results also provide novel insights into the basis of mnemonic decisions in older adults. Specifically, we demonstrate that trial-wise indices of reinstatement strength — indexed using classifier-derived evidence and encoding-retrieval pattern similarity — were tightly linked to memory behaviour, including response accuracy and speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by trial-wise analyses showing relationships between reinstatement strength and both accuracy and reaction time.

claim: Retrieval was not 'all or none', but likely graded.
source: This finding suggests that retrieval was not 'all or none', but likely graded (Mickes et al., 2009; Kuhl et al., 2011; Harlow and Yonelinas, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the graded relationship between reinstatement strength and memory behavior, interpreted in the context of prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Correct category judgments could be supported by retrieval of generic category information, prototypical details, specific exemplar details, or even retrieval of erroneous, but category consistent details.
source: Indeed, while participants were instructed during scanning to recollect the specific associate, correct category judgments (agnostic to correct exemplar-specific recall) could nonetheless be supported by retrieval of generic category information (e.g., a place), prototypical details (e.g., a bridge), specific exemplar details (e.g., the Golden Gate Bridge), or even retrieval of erroneous, but category consistent details (e.g., Niagara Falls).
evidence: This is speculation about the different types of information that could support correct category judgments.

claim: The category-level reinstatement effects observed likely reflect some combination of different retrieval outcomes.
source: The category-level reinstatement effects observed here likely reflect some combination of these retrieval outcomes, as suggested by the strong correlation between post-scan exemplar-specific recall and within-scan associative d', along with the observation that the proportion of specific exemplars recalled post-scan was generally lower than correct categorical judgements during scanning (though the former undoubtedly declined due to the longer retention interval and interference effects).
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing the relationship between in-scanner and post-scan memory performance.

claim: VTC and ANG may support representations of distinct types of event features (e.g., perceptual features in VTC and semantic and/or multimodal features in ANG).
source: One possibility, though speculative, is that VTC and ANG support representations of distinct types of event features (e.g., perceptual features in VTC and semantic and/or multimodal features in ANG). This possibility is in line with existing evidence (e.g., Bonnici et al., 2016; Favila et al., 2018) and also with the present observation that reinstatement strength in VTC and ANG made complementary contributions to retrieval success.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional roles of different brain regions, supported by citations to prior work and the present findings.

claim: Recovery of stronger mnemonic evidence was associated with greater accuracy and faster responses for representations supported by VTC and ANG alike.
source: Regardless of the precise nature of the details recalled, we demonstrate that, as in younger adults (Kuhl et al., 2011; Kuhl et al., 2013; Gordon et al., 2014), recovery of stronger mnemonic evidence was associated with greater accuracy and faster responses, and this was true for representations supported by VTC and ANG alike.
evidence: This claim is supported by trial-wise analyses showing relationships between reinstatement strength and behavior in both regions.

claim: The relationship between reinstatement strength and behavior may reflect reduced demands on post-retrieval monitoring and selection processes and/or greater confidence in the face of stronger mnemonic evidence.
source: This relationship may reflect reduced demands on post-retrieval monitoring and selection processes and/or greater confidence in the face of stronger mnemonic evidence.
evidence: This is speculation about the cognitive mechanisms underlying the relationship between reinstatement strength and behavior.

claim: The weakening of the trial-level relationship between VTC reinstatement strength and behaviour with increased age could be related to age-related changes in decision criteria, retrieval monitoring ability, response strategies, or some combination of these factors.
source: Interestingly, the strength of the trial-level relationship between VTC reinstatement strength and behaviour weakened with increased age. This could be related to age-related changes in decision criteria, retrieval monitoring ability, response strategies, or some combination of these factors.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying the age moderation effect.

claim: The effect of age on reinstatement strength was observed after accounting for variance in encoding classifier performance.
source: Importantly, the effect of age on reinstatement strength, and the relationship between reinstatement strength and memory performance, was observed after accounting for variance in encoding classifier performance, a putative assay of cortical differentiation (i.e., the ability to establish distinct neural patterns associated with different visual stimulus categories) during memory encoding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical approach of controlling for encoding classifier strength in the analyses.

claim: Prior work has demonstrated reductions in cortical differentiation in older relative to young adults.
source: Prior work has demonstrated reductions in cortical differentiation in older relative to young adults (Voss et al., 2008; Carp et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Koen et al., 2019; Trelle et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on age-related changes in cortical differentiation.

claim: Evidence from both older and young adults suggests that cortical differentiation at encoding can impact reinstatement strength and memory performance.
source: and evidence from both older and young adults suggests that cortical differentiation at encoding can impact reinstatement strength (Gordon et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2015) and memory performance (Koen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research showing relationships between encoding differentiation and retrieval outcomes.

claim: Encoding classifier strength was a strong predictor of category-level reinstatement strength in the present sample.
source: Indeed, we found that encoding classifier strength was a strong predictor of category-level reinstatement strength in the present sample.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analyses showing the relationship between encoding and retrieval classifier strength.

claim: By controlling for encoding strength in the current analyses, the observed variance in reinstatement strength does not simply reflect downstream effects of cortical differentiation.
source: Critically, by controlling for encoding strength in the current analyses, the present results indicate that the observed variance in reinstatement strength, and its relation to memory performance, does not simply reflect downstream effects of cortical differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical approach of controlling for encoding strength.

claim: Variance in reinstatement strength likely also provides information about the precision with which event representations are retrieved in older adults.
source: Instead, variance in reinstatement strength likely also provides information about the precision with which event representations are retrieved in older adults.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that reinstatement strength explains variance beyond encoding differentiation.

claim: The data provide neuroimaging evidence in support of existing proposals that age-related episodic memory decline is driven, in part, by a loss of specificity or precision in mnemonic representations.
source: These data therefore provide neuroimaging evidence in support of existing proposals that age-related episodic memory decline is driven, in part, by a loss of specificity or precision in mnemonic representations, a possibility that has been well-supported by behavioural evidence (Luo and Craik, 2009; Trelle et al., 2017; Korkki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings regarding reinstatement strength and memory performance, interpreted in the context of prior behavioral work.

claim: Hippocampal activity may signal recollection of some event details, but this signal alone may not indicate the fidelity or precision with which the event is recollected.
source: One possibility is that hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement strength index distinct aspects of recollection: retrieval success vs. retrieval precision, respectively (e.g., Harlow and Yonelinas, 2016; Richter et al., 2016). That is, whereas increases in hippocampal activity may signal recollection of some event details, this signal alone may not indicate the fidelity or precision with which the event is recollected.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of hippocampal activity, supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Reinstatement strength may provide more information about the contents of recollection, including the specificity or precision of mnemonic representations.
source: Conversely, reinstatement strength may provide more information about the contents of recollection, including the specificity or precision of mnemonic representations (e.g., recall of generic as opposed to exemplar-specific details), and perhaps even the nature of the details recollected (i.e., perceptual vs semantic).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of reinstatement strength.

claim: Representations reinstated in cortex may be differentially affected by top-down goal states, post-retrieval monitoring, selection and/or decision processes.
source: An alternative, but not mutually exclusive possibility, is that representations reinstated in cortex may be differentially affected by top-down goal states, post-retrieval monitoring, selection and/or decision processes (Kuhl et al., 2013; Favila et al., 2018), which may contribute unique variance in memory performance beyond that explained by hippocampal-initiated event replay.
evidence: This is speculation about factors that may influence cortical reinstatement, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Variability in episodic remembering, and variability in the strength of pattern completion metrics, is likely influenced by a number of variables, only some of which are measured here.
source: Indeed, it is important to note that variability in episodic remembering, and indeed variability in the strength of the present pattern completion metrics, is likely influenced by a number of variables, only some of which are measured here.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study and the complexity of factors influencing memory.

claim: Aging may affect other processes at retrieval, including elaboration of retrieval cues and post-retrieval monitoring and selection.
source: For example, aging may affect other processes at retrieval, including elaboration of retrieval cues (Morcom and Rugg, 2004) and post-retrieval monitoring and selection (McDonough et al., 2013; Trelle et al., 2019)
evidence: This is speculation about other age-related changes that may affect memory, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Aging may affect factors at encoding, including the differentiation of stimulus representations, goal-directed or sustained attention, and elaborative or 'strategic' encoding processes.
source: as well as factors at encoding, including the differentiation of stimulus representations (Voss et al., 2008; Carp et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Koen et al., 2019; Trelle et al., 2019), goal-directed or sustained attention (Hultsch et al., 2002; Geerligs et al., 2014), and elaborative or 'strategic' encoding processes (Luo et al., 2007; Trelle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about other age-related changes that may affect memory, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hippocampal and cortical indices of pattern completion play a central role in determining whether individual events will be remembered or forgotten.
source: Nevertheless, the present results provide compelling initial evidence that (a) hippocampal and cortical indices of pattern completion play a central role in determining whether individual events will be remembered or forgotten
evidence: This is an inference based on the trial-wise findings showing relationships between neural measures and memory outcomes.

claim: Predicted relationships between hippocampal activity, reinstatement strength, and associative memory retrieval can be observed even late in the lifespan.
source: (b) that predicted relationships between hippocampal activity, reinstatement strength, and associative memory retrieval can be observed even late in the lifespan
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings in older adults showing the expected relationships.

claim: Neural metrics of pattern completion explain unique variance in memory performance across individuals.
source: and (c) and that these neural metrics explain unique variance in memory performance across individuals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the individual differences analyses showing independent contributions of neural measures.

claim: The relationship between neural measures and standardized neuropsychological test measures suggests that the neural indices derived from task-based fMRI are tapping into stable individual differences.
source: The relationship between these measures, collected during separate testing sessions, suggests that the neural indices derived from task-based fMRI are tapping into stable individual differences, and may represent a sensitive biomarker of hippocampal and cortical function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that neural measures predict standardized test performance collected in a separate session.

claim: Neural indices of pattern completion may represent a sensitive biomarker of hippocampal and cortical function.
source: The relationship between these measures, collected during separate testing sessions, suggests that the neural indices derived from task-based fMRI are tapping into stable individual differences, and may represent a sensitive biomarker of hippocampal and cortical function.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential utility of these neural measures as biomarkers.

claim: Neural indices provide information that cannot be garnered from paper and pencil tests alone.
source: Critically, we also demonstrate that these neural and neuropsychological test measures explained unique variance in associative memory, together accounting for 50% of the variance in exemplar-specific recall across individuals. This not only indicates that the present neural indices provide information that cannot be garnered from paper and pencil tests alone
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that neural measures explain variance beyond standardized test performance.

claim: Combining neural metrics with existing measurement tools can build more accurate models to explain individual differences in memory performance in older adults.
source: but also suggests that we can combine these neural metrics with existing measurement tools to build more accurate models to explain individual differences in memory performance in older adults.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that neural and behavioral measures together explain substantial variance in memory performance.

claim: Combining task-related neural measures with other known biomarkers of brain health and disease risk may further increase sensitivity for explaining individual differences in memory performance and predicting future disease risk and memory decline.
source: An important direction for future work is to assess whether combining task-related neural measures, such as those identified here, with other known biomarkers of brain health and disease risk (e.g., in vivo measures of amyloid and tau accumulation, hippocampal volume, white matter integrity; Hedden et al., 2016; Jack et al., 2018) can further increase sensitivity for explaining individual differences in memory performance, as well as predicting future disease risk and memory decline prior to the emergence of clinical impairment.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions, supported by citations to prior work on biomarkers.

claim: Hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval provide a partial account for why and when older adults remember.
source: By exploring how neural indices of pattern completion vary — both across trials and across individuals — these findings demonstrate that hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval provide a partial account for why and when older adults remember
evidence: This is an inference based on the trial-wise and individual differences findings.

claim: Neural indices of pattern completion predict which older adults will perform better than others across multiple widely adopted assays of episodic memory.
source: and they predict which older adults will perform better than others across multiple widely adopted assays of episodic memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the individual differences findings showing relationships between neural measures and multiple memory outcomes.

claim: Some neural indices of pattern completion may be affected by age to a greater degree than others.
source: They also suggest that some neural indices of pattern completion may be affected by age to a greater degree than others, though we note that both the presence and absence of age effects must be interpreted with caution due to the cross-sectional nature of the study design, and should be confirmed in the context of longitudinal studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential age effects observed for different neural measures, with appropriate caution about the cross-sectional design.

claim: The high within-group variance in brain and behavior among cognitively normal older adults likely contributes to the wealth of mixed findings in the literature.
source: Nevertheless, our findings underscore the striking heterogeneity in brain and behaviour, even among cognitively normal older adults, and lend support to the hypothesis that this high within-group variance likely contributes to the wealth of mixed findings in the literature, particularly for traditional group-level comparisons in the context of small-to-moderate sample sizes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed individual differences and the context of prior mixed findings in the literature.

claim: An individual differences approach can advance understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying variability in episodic memory in older adults.
source: Collectively, our findings illustrate how an individual differences approach can advance understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying variability in episodic memory in older adults.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall findings of the study demonstrating the value of the individual differences approach.

claim: One hundred and five cognitively healthy older adults (aged 60–82 years; 65 female) participated as part of the Stanford Aging and Memory Study.
source: One hundred and five cognitively healthy older adults (aged 60–82 years; 65 female) participated as part of the Stanford Aging and Memory Study.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Data from five participants were excluded from all analyses due to excess head motion during scanning, yielding a final sample of 100 older adults.
source: Data from five participants were excluded from all analyses due to excess head motion during scanning (see fMRI pre-processing), yielding a final sample of 100 older adults (60–82 years; 61 female; see Table 1 for demographics).
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criteria and final sample size.

claim: Participants completed a neuropsychological test battery consisting of standardized tests assessing a range of cognitive functions.
source: Participants completed a neuropsychological test battery consisting of standardized tests assessing a range of cognitive functions, including episodic memory, executive function, visuospatial processing, language, and attention.
evidence: This is a description of the neuropsychological assessment procedures.

claim: A composite delayed recall score was computed for each participant by z-scoring and averaging delayed recall subtest scores from the Logical Memory, HVLT-R, and BVMT-R.
source: Subsequently, a composite delayed recall score was computed for each participant by (a) z-scoring the delayed recall subtest scores from the Logical Memory (LM) subtest of the Wechsler Memory Scale, 3rd edition (WMS-III; Wechsler, 1997), Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT-R; Brandt, 1991), and the Brief Visuospatial Memory Test-Revised (BVMT-R; Benedict, 1997), and (b) then averaging.
evidence: This is a description of how the delayed recall composite score was computed.

claim: The delayed recall composite score declined with age (β = −0.21, p < 0.005).
source: This composite score declined with age (β = −0.21, p < 0.005)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the delayed recall composite score.

claim: The delayed recall composite score was lower in males than females (β = −0.35, p < 0.05).
source: was lower in males than females (β = −0.35, p < 0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing a sex effect on the delayed recall composite score.

claim: The delayed recall composite score did not vary with years of education (β = 0.07, p > 0.31).
source: but did not vary with years of education (β = 0.07, p > 0.31).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant education effect on the delayed recall composite score.

claim: Stimuli comprised words paired with colour photos of faces and scenes obtained from online sources.
source: Stimuli comprised words paired with colour photos of faces and scenes obtained from online sources.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: For each participant, 120 words were randomly selected and paired with pictures during a study phase, and these 120 words plus 30 remaining words (foils) appeared as cues during the retrieval phase.
source: For each participant, 120 words (out of 150 words total) were randomly selected and paired with the pictures (60 word-face; 60 word-place) during a study phase, and these 120 words plus the remaining 30 words (foils) appeared as cues during the retrieval phase.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants performed an associative memory task consisting of five rounds of alternating encoding and retrieval blocks.
source: Next, concurrent with fMRI, participants performed an associative memory task consisting of five rounds of alternating encoding and retrieval blocks (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task, visualized in Figure 1.

claim: In each encoding block, participants viewed 24 word-picture pairs and were asked to intentionally form an association between each word and picture pair.
source: In each encoding block, participants viewed 24 word-picture pairs (12 word-face and 12 word-place) and were asked to intentionally form an association between each word and picture pair.
evidence: This is a description of the encoding task.

claim: In each retrieval block, 24 target words were interspersed with 6 novel (foil) words; participants made a 4-way memory decision for each word.
source: Following each encoding block, participants performed a retrieval task that probed item recognition and associative recollection. In each block, 24 target words were interspersed with 6 novel (foil) words; participants made a 4-way memory decision for each word.
evidence: This is a description of the retrieval task.

claim: After the MR scan session, a final overt cued-recall test was conducted outside the scanner to evaluate the degree to which participants were able to recollect the specific face or place associated with each target word.
source: After the MR scan session, a final overt cued-recall test was conducted outside the scanner to evaluate the degree to which participants were able to recollect the specific face or place associated with each target word.
evidence: This is a description of the post-scan memory test.

claim: Data were acquired on a 3T GE Discovery MR750 MRI scanner using a 32-channel radiofrequency receive-only head coil.
source: Data were acquired on a 3T GE Discovery MR750 MRI scanner (GE Healthcare) using a 32-channel radiofrequency receive-only head coil (Nova Medical).
evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional data were acquired using a multiband EPI sequence (acceleration factor = 3) consisting of 63 oblique axial slices parallel to the long axis of the hippocampus.
source: Functional data were acquired using a multiband EPI sequence (acceleration factor = 3) consisting of 63 oblique axial slices parallel to the long axis of the hippocampus (TR = 2 s, TE = 30 ms, FoV = 215 mm x 215 mm, flip angle = 74, voxel size = 1.8 × 1.8 × 2 mm).
evidence: This is a description of the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: The hippocampal mask was defined manually using each participant's high-resolution T2-weighted structural image.
source: The hippocampal mask was defined manually using each participant's high-resolution T2-weighted structural image using established procedures (Olsen et al., 2009), and comprised the whole hippocampus (see Figure 4—figure supplements 5–6 for analysis of hippocampal subfields).
evidence: This is a description of the ROI definition procedures.

claim: The VTC mask was composed of three anatomical regions: parahippocampal cortex, fusiform gyrus, and inferior temporal cortex.
source: The VTC mask was composed of three anatomical regions: parahippocampal cortex, fusiform gyrus, and inferior temporal cortex.
evidence: This is a description of the VTC ROI definition.

claim: The ANG ROI was defined by the intersection of the Freesurfer inferior parietal lobe label and the Default Network of the Yeo 7 network atlas.
source: The ANG ROI was defined by the intersection of the Freesurfer inferior parietal lobe label and the Default Network of the Yeo 7 network atlas (Yeo et al., 2011), defined on the Freesurfer average (fsaverage) cortical surface mesh.
evidence: This is a description of the ANG ROI definition.

claim: Classification was implemented using L2-penalized logistic regression models.
source: Classification was implemented using Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), nilearn (Abraham et al., 2014), nibabel (Brett et al., 2016), and in house Python scripts, and performed using L2-penalized logistic regression models as instantiated in the LIBLINEAR classification library (regularization parameter C = 1).
evidence: This is a description of the classification analysis methods.

claim: A feature selection step was conducted, in which a subject-specific univariate contrast was used to identify the top 250 voxels that were most sensitive to each category during encoding, yielding a set of 500 voxels over which classification analyses were performed.
source: A feature selection step was also conducted, in which a subject-specific univariate contrast was used to identify the top 250 voxels that were most sensitive to each category (face, place) during encoding, yielding a set of 500 voxels over which classification analyses were performed.
evidence: This is a description of the feature selection procedure for classification analysis.

claim: To measure category-level cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval, a classifier was trained on all encoding phase data, and then tested on all retrieval phase data.
source: To measure category-level cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval, we trained a new classifier on all encoding phase data, and then tested on all retrieval phase data.
evidence: This is a description of the classification analysis approach for measuring reinstatement.

claim: The significance of classifier performance for each condition and ROI was assessed using permutation testing.
source: The significance of classifier performance for each condition and ROI was assessed using permutation testing. We generated a null distribution for each participant by shuffling the trial labels over 1000 iterations for each of the 10 subsampling iterations, calculating mean classifier accuracy for each iteration.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical approach for assessing classifier significance.

claim: Pattern similarity analyses were used to measure event-level cortical reinstatement by computing the similarity (Pearson correlation) between trial-wise activity patterns extracted from ROIs during encoding and retrieval.
source: To complement the classification analyses, we used pattern similarity analyses to measure event-level cortical reinstatement. This approach involved computing the similarity (Pearson correlation) between trial-wise activity patterns extracted from ROIs during encoding and retrieval (i.e., encoding-retrieval similarity; ERS).
evidence: This is a description of the pattern similarity analysis approach.

claim: Trial-wise analyses were conducted using mixed effects models (linear and logistic).
source: All statistical analyses were implemented in the R environment (version 3.4.4). Trial-wise analyses were conducted using mixed effects models (linear and logistic) using the lmer4 statistical package (Bates et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach for trial-wise data.
